passage:
Counsellor's note, Monday. Tushar brought his five-year-old, Mini, to see me the day after Mini's Dada died. Tushar did not say Dada was "sleeping" or "gone away". Sitting at Mini's height, he said, "Dada's body stopped working. He was very old and very tired. He cannot return. We are sad and we can cry."
Mini asked, "Will Dada come for my birthday?" Tushar answered gently, "No, Mini. He can't come." Mini asked it twice more that afternoon and Tushar said the same words each time. Mini's shoulders eased. Then Mini asked for a biscuit.
Tenzin, school counsellor

qa.q: How old is Mini?
qa.a: Mini is five years old.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling while telling Mini that Dada would not come back?
qa.a: Tushar was probably sad and determined to be honest, since Tushar chose plain words at Mini's height. Coming in the day after the death shows how much it mattered.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that helped Mini understand?
qa.a: Tushar used plain words such as "Dada's body stopped working" and "He cannot return", not "sleeping". He repeated the same answer patiently when Mini asked again.

qa.q: What might Mini have been feeling when asking whether Dada would come for the birthday?
qa.a: Mini was probably confused and a little afraid, trying to understand what had happened. Asking again shows a need to be sure.

grounding: A man tells his five-year-old that Dada's body stopped working and Dada cannot return, without euphemisms, and answers repeated questions.

passage:
On the verandah, Usha sat with her son Vaibhav, five, after the funeral ashes were done. The house was full of relatives talking low.
"Vaibhav, Nana's body stopped working. Nana died. He will not wake up, and he cannot return."
Vaibhav frowned. "Is Nana sleeping?"
"No, beta. Sleeping bodies wake up. Nana's body has stopped. It doesn't hurt him now."
"Will you die?"
Usha took a breath. "One day, when I am very old. Not soon. I am here now."
Vaibhav leaned on her shoulder. Later, in the yard, he asked the same question again, and Usha answered the same way.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav ask when Usha told him Nana's body had stopped working?
qa.a: Vaibhav asked, "Is Nana sleeping?"

qa.q: What was Usha feeling while answering "Will you die?"
qa.a: Usha seemed sad but steady, taking a breath and answering calmly. Saying "I am here now" shows the wish to make Vaibhav feel safe.

qa.q: What did Usha do that made the explanation easier for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Usha said plainly that Nana died, explained that sleeping bodies wake up but Nana's has stopped, and stayed close. She gave the same answer when the question came again.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when asking "Will you die?"
qa.a: Vaibhav was worried and afraid of losing Usha too. The question and leaning on the shoulder show a need to feel safe.

grounding: A woman tells her son plainly that Nana's body stopped working and Nana cannot return, without saying Nana is sleeping.

passage:
In their Nairobi home, Wanjiru, five, kept asking when Guka would come back from the hospital.
Her father, Tomas, sat on the floor beside her. "Wanjiru, Guka died. His body stopped working. It can't breathe or eat or feel pain anymore. He won't come back."
"Is he sleeping?"
"No, it's not like sleeping. Sleeping people wake up. Guka won't."
She was quiet. Then, "Will he come for my birthday?"
"No, love. But we can remember him on your birthday."
The next morning she asked again. Tomas answered again, just as gently.

qa.q: Where had Guka been?
qa.a: Guka had been in the hospital.

qa.q: Why did Wanjiru keep asking the same question?
qa.a: Wanjiru was confused and sad, and asking again was how she tried to understand that Guka was not coming back.

qa.q: Which of Tomas's choices helped Wanjiru, and why?
qa.a: He used plain words, said clearly it was not like sleeping, and answered her repeated questions gently each time.

qa.q: What was it like for Tomas to explain this?
qa.a: It was likely painful and tender for Tomas, grieving Guka himself while staying calm and patient for her.

grounding: A parent explains in plain words that grandpa's body stopped working and he will not come back, and answers repeated questions.

passage:
In the hospital's quiet family room, Jagdish, the nurse, brought Wasim a cup of warm milk and left the door half open.
Abbu knelt in front of Wasim. "Beta, Dada died this morning. His body stopped working. His heart stopped, and he can't breathe anymore. He won't come back home."
"Is he sleeping in there?"
"No. Sleeping is different. When you sleep, you wake up. Dada won't wake up."
Wasim stared at the milk. "Did it hurt?"
"No, beta. He can't feel anything now."
"Can I still talk about him?"
"Always."

qa.q: What did Jagdish bring Wasim?
qa.a: Jagdish brought Wasim a cup of warm milk.

qa.q: What was Wasim worried about when he asked if it hurt?
qa.a: Wasim was scared that Dada had been in pain, and wanted to know he was not suffering.

qa.q: What made Abbu's explanation helpful?
qa.a: He knelt, used plain words about the body stopping, explained that death is not sleep, and answered each question simply.

qa.q: How might Jagdish, the nurse, see the moment?
qa.a: Jagdish likely felt quiet compassion, giving the family privacy with the half-open door and the milk.

grounding: A parent tells a child plainly that grandfather's body stopped working and he will not come back, without the word sleeping.

passage:
I'm Urmila, and I live across the courtyard from Pema's family in Darjeeling. The day after her grandfather died, I saw her mother sit with Pema on the steps, both in warm jackets.
I heard her say, "Popo's body stopped working, Pema. He died. He won't come back."
Pema asked, "Did he go to sleep?"
"No. Sleep is different. He isn't sleeping."
Pema was quiet, then asked where Popo's slippers would go. Her mother said they could keep them.
Later that week I heard Pema ask again, "Is Popo coming back?" Her mother answered the same way, calmly.

qa.q: Where does Urmila live?
qa.a: Urmila lives across the courtyard from Pema's family in Darjeeling.

qa.q: What does Pema's question about the slippers suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Pema was sad and trying to make sense of the loss through something familiar, wondering about the things Popo left behind.

qa.q: Why did the mother's plain words work well?
qa.a: They made clear that Popo died and is not sleeping, which avoids fear of sleep, and she answered calmly each time Pema asked again.

qa.q: How does Urmila see the mother's approach?
qa.a: Urmila notices and seems to admire her calm, gentle patience with Pema's repeated questions.

grounding: An observer watches a parent tell a child in plain words that grandfather's body stopped working, and answer repeated questions.

passage:
Monday: Tarun asked why everyone was crying. Pappa knelt. "Appachan died. His body stopped working. He won't come back. It isn't like sleeping." Tarun held Pappa's hand tight.
Wednesday: "Is Appachan coming for my birthday?" Pappa, Jomon, answered again, gently. "No, monu. His body stopped working. We can miss him together."
Saturday: Tarun asked a third time, then added, "Will you stop working?" "Not for a long, long time, I hope," Jomon said, and they looked at Appachan's old spectacles together.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask on Wednesday?
qa.a: Is Appachan coming for my birthday?

qa.q: What does Tarun's question "Will you stop working?" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Tarun is afraid of losing Pappa too, now that he understands Appachan will not come back.

qa.q: Why were Jomon's words helpful for Tarun?
qa.a: Plain words like "his body stopped working" and "he won't come back", instead of calling it sleep, gave Tarun a clear and less frightening picture.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jomon to answer the same question again?
qa.a: Jomon is grieving too, yet stays gentle and patient, treating each repeated question as normal.

grounding: Shows a parent telling a young child in plain words that grandpa's body stopped working and he will not come back, and answering the same question again on later days.
